title: Meet Minh Anh
text:
Hello! My name is Minh Anh. I am nineteen years old and I am a first-year student at a university in Can Tho. I study business. I live in a small apartment near the university with my cousin, Thu.

Every morning, I get up at six o'clock and ride my bike to school. My classes start at seven. In the afternoon, I work part-time at a bookstore. I love reading, so it is a great job for me.

On weekends, I visit my parents in Vinh Long. My mother is a teacher and my father is a farmer. I have one younger brother. His name is Bao and he is in grade 8.

title: Nam's email from Da Lat
text:

I'm in Da Lat with my family now. We arrived yesterday afternoon. The weather here is cool and sunny, but it is cold at night, so I always wear a jacket. Our hotel is small but very clean, and it is near Xuan Huong Lake.

This morning, we walked around the lake and had breakfast at a market. The strawberries here are delicious! Tomorrow we are going to visit a flower garden. We are going home on Sunday.

See you soon,
Nam

title: Mr. Tam, the bus driver
text:
Mr. Tam is a bus driver in Can Tho. He is forty-five years old. He gets up at 4:30 every morning because his first bus leaves at 5:30. He drives bus number 7 from the city center to the university. He drives the same route eight times a day.

Mr. Tam likes his job because he meets a lot of people. Many students know him and say hello every morning. But his job is not easy. The traffic is often heavy, and he sometimes works on weekends.

He finishes work at 3 p.m. Then he picks up his daughter from school.

text:

My father, Mr. Hai, is an engineer. He works for a big company in Ho Chi Minh City, so he is often away from home. My mother is a nurse at a hospital near our house. My grandmother is seventy years old. She cooks very well, and she makes lunch for us every day.

title: Hoi An
text:
Hoi An is a small old town in central Vietnam. It is about 30 kilometers from Da Nang. Many tourists visit Hoi An every year.

The town has old yellow houses, small streets and a famous bridge called the Japanese Bridge. In the evening, people put colorful lanterns on the river, and the town looks very beautiful. You can also eat many local dishes, such as cao lau and banh mi.

The best time to visit is from February to April because the weather is not too hot and it does not rain much. Hoi An is very busy in the summer, so hotels are more expensive then.

title: Grandma's smartphone
text:
Last month, my grandmother turned seventy, and my parents gave her a smartphone. At first, she didn't like it. The screen was too small for her, and she didn't know how to use the apps. She said, "My old phone was better!"

So every evening, I sat with her and taught her one new thing. First, she learned how to make video calls. Then she learned how to take photos and send messages. I also made the letters on the screen bigger.

Now she loves her phone. She video-calls my aunt in Australia every Sunday and sends photos of her garden to our family group. Yesterday, she even sent me a funny sticker!

title: A trip to Ha Giang
text:
Last October, my friends and I went on a four-day motorbike trip in Ha Giang, in the north of Vietnam. We flew from Can Tho to Hanoi and then took an overnight bus to Ha Giang city. There, we rented motorbikes and hired a local guide named Sung.

The roads were narrow and there were many mountains, so we drove slowly. The views were amazing, especially at Ma Pi Leng Pass. At night, we stayed in homestays and ate dinner with local families. On the third day, it rained heavily and we couldn't drive, so we stayed in the village and learned how to weave cloth from the local women.

It was a tiring trip, but it was the best trip of my life. I want to go back next year.

title: Student sleep survey
text:
STUDENT SLEEP SURVEY

Last month, the Student Union asked 200 students at our college about their sleep. Here are the results:

- 40% of students sleep less than 6 hours a night.
- 45% sleep 6 to 8 hours.
- Only 15% sleep more than 8 hours.
- 70% of students use their phones in bed before sleeping.
- The most common reasons for going to bed late are homework (35%), social media (30%) and part-time jobs (20%).

Doctors say young adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night, so many students at our college do not get enough sleep. The Student Union suggests turning off phones 30 minutes before bedtime.

text:

title: How Long improved his English
text:
Hoang Long is a 21-year-old IT student. Two years ago, his English was very weak. He could read a little, but he couldn't speak at all. He wanted to work for an international company, so he decided to change.

First, he watched English videos about technology every day with English subtitles. Then he joined an English speaking club at his university. At the beginning, he was shy and only listened. After a few months, he started to talk more. He also practiced with a free app for 15 minutes before bed.

Now Long can have simple conversations in English, and last month he gave a short presentation in English in front of 50 people. His advice is: "Practice a little every day, and don't be afraid of making mistakes."

title: Tet in Vietnam
text:
Tet, or Lunar New Year, is the most important holiday in Vietnam. It usually happens in late January or February.

Before Tet, people clean and decorate their houses with peach blossoms in the north or yellow apricot blossoms in the south. They also buy new clothes and cook special food such as banh chung or banh tet.

During Tet, families get together. Children wear new clothes and wish their grandparents good health. Then adults give them lucky money in red envelopes. People also visit relatives, friends and temples.

Many people who work in big cities travel back to their hometowns for Tet, so buses and trains are very crowded at this time.

title: An interview with a chef
text:
Interviewer: Chef Minh, how did you become a chef?
Chef Minh: When I was a child, I often helped my mother in her small restaurant. I loved watching her cook. After high school, I studied at a cooking school in Ho Chi Minh City for two years.
Interviewer: What is a normal day like for you?
Chef Minh: I go to the market at 5 a.m. to buy fresh fish and vegetables. Then I prepare the food with my team. The restaurant opens at 11, and we finish at about 10 p.m. It's a long day!
Interviewer: What's your favorite dish to cook?
Chef Minh: Canh chua – sour fish soup. It's simple, but it reminds me of my mother.
Interviewer: Do you have any advice for young people who want to be chefs?
Chef Minh: Be patient and work hard. And always use fresh ingredients.

title: A Saturday diary
text:
Saturday, May 10th

Today was a busy but fun day. In the morning, I got up late, at 9 o'clock. After breakfast, I cleaned my room and washed my clothes. At 11, my best friend, Ha, came to my house, and we cooked lunch together. We made fried noodles, but we put too much salt in them!

In the afternoon, we went to the bookstore. Ha bought a novel, and I bought a dictionary for my English class. Then it started to rain, so we stayed in a café for two hours and talked.

In the evening, I watched a movie with my family. Now I'm tired, but I'm happy. Tomorrow I have to do my homework.

title: Ca Mau and Ho Chi Minh City
text:
I'm Duy. I grew up in Ca Mau, a small city in the far south of Vietnam, but now I study in Ho Chi Minh City. The two places are very different.

Ho Chi Minh City is much bigger and busier than Ca Mau. There are more shopping malls, more restaurants and more jobs. However, the traffic is worse and the air is more polluted. Life there is also more expensive: my small room costs three times more than a big room in Ca Mau.

Ca Mau is quieter and greener. People there are very friendly, and the seafood is the freshest I have ever eaten.

I like the big city because there are more opportunities, but after I graduate, I want to go back to Ca Mau and open a small business.

title: Quynh, the hospital volunteer
text:
Every Sunday morning, Quynh, a 20-year-old nursing student, volunteers at a children's hospital in Can Tho. She started two years ago because her little brother stayed in this hospital for a month when he was sick. She remembers that he was often bored and sad.

At the hospital, Quynh and the other volunteers read stories, draw pictures and play games with the children. Sometimes they sing songs together. The children call her "Sister Quynh".

Volunteering is not always easy. Some children are very sick, and Quynh feels sad. But she says the children's smiles make her happy. She also thinks the experience will help her become a better nurse in the future.

title: Food delivery apps: convenient, but at what cost?
text:
Ten years ago, if you wanted a bowl of pho at home, you had to go out and buy it yourself. Today, many people in Vietnamese cities simply open an app on their phone, choose a dish and wait for it to arrive at their door.

Food delivery apps have become extremely popular, especially among students and young office workers. In a survey of 400 young people in Can Tho, carried out by a group of university students, more than 60% of them said they order food online at least once a week. The main reason is convenience: people are busy, and the apps save them time.

However, not everyone is happy about this trend. Some small restaurant owners say the apps take up to 25% of the price of each order, so they earn much less money. Environmental groups are also worried about the huge number of plastic boxes, bags and spoons that are thrown away every day.

Some apps are now trying to solve this problem. Customers can choose "no plastic cutlery" when they order, and a few restaurants give a small discount to people who bring their own containers. It is a small step, but it shows that the industry is starting to listen.

title: My first semester in Busan
text:
When I arrived in Busan last September, I could only say "hello" and "thank you" in Korean. I had studied the language online for three months, but real conversations were much faster than the videos I had watched.

The first few weeks were difficult. I got lost on the subway twice, and once I ordered a very spicy dish because I couldn't read the menu. I also missed Vietnamese food and my family a lot, especially at dinner time.

Things got better when I joined the university's international students' club. Every Friday, we cook food from our home countries and share it. I have made friends from Japan, Indonesia and Mexico, and we usually speak English together. A Korean classmate, Jiwoo, also offered to help me with my Korean if I helped her with English. Now we meet twice a week at a café near the campus.

After four months, my Korean is still far from perfect, but I can take the bus, go shopping and chat with my neighbors without much trouble. My advice for anyone who wants to study abroad: don't be afraid of making mistakes, and say "yes" to every chance to meet new people.

– Ha My

title: A peaceful stay by the river
text:
★★★★☆ Reviewed by Lucy (UK)

My husband and I spent three nights at Bay Lan Homestay in Cai Be, and overall we had a lovely time. The homestay is a traditional wooden house surrounded by fruit trees, about ten minutes by boat from the town center.

The best thing about our stay was the family who run it. Mr. Bay and his wife treated us like their own children. On our second evening, they taught us how to make spring rolls, and we all had dinner together. The food was simple but delicious, and everything came from their own garden.

Our room was clean and comfortable, although it was a little hot at night because there was only a fan, not air conditioning. Also, if you are a light sleeper, be prepared: the roosters start crowing at about 4:30 every morning!

The price was very reasonable – 600,000 dong per night, including breakfast and a bicycle. I would definitely recommend this place to anyone who wants to experience real life in the Mekong Delta, but it might not suit travelers who need modern comforts.

title: The lost wallet
text:
Last Tuesday, Phuc, a second-year engineering student, was riding his bike home from the library when he saw a brown wallet lying in the middle of the road. He stopped and picked it up. Inside, there were two million dong, a bank card and an ID card belonging to a woman called Nguyen Thi Thu.

At first, Phuc didn't know what to do. Two million dong was more than he earned in a month from his part-time job. But he thought about how worried the owner must be. "If I lost my wallet, I would want someone to return it," he said later.

The ID card showed an address in An Binh Ward, about three kilometers away. Phuc rode there immediately, but nobody was home. A neighbor told him that Mrs. Thu worked at a pharmacy nearby, so he went there and found her.

Mrs. Thu was so grateful that she started crying. She had been looking for the wallet all afternoon, because the money was for her son's school fees. She tried to give Phuc 500,000 dong as a reward, but he refused. "I just did what anyone should do," he said with a smile.

title: Green Cup: a café without plastic
text:
Reporter: Hoang Anh, when did you open Green Cup?
Hoang Anh: In March 2024, just after I graduated. I studied business, and I had always dreamed of running my own café.

Reporter: What makes Green Cup different from other cafés?
Hoang Anh: We don't use any single-use plastic. Drinks come in glass cups if you sit in, and if you want a takeaway, you can bring your own cup or borrow one of ours. You just return it next time.

Reporter: Do customers really return the cups?
Hoang Anh: Most of them do! In the first month, we lost about 30 cups, so I was worried. But now we lose fewer than five a month. People like the idea, and regular customers remind each other.

Reporter: What was the hardest part of starting the business?
Hoang Anh: Money, definitely. My parents lent me some, but I also had to borrow from a bank. For the first eight months, I didn't pay myself any salary at all.

Reporter: What advice would you give to young people who want to start a business?
Hoang Anh: Start small and listen to your customers. My first idea was to sell cakes too, but nobody bought them, so I stopped and focused on drinks.

title: Young volunteers clean up Can Tho's canals
text:
On the first Sunday of every month, about fifty young people meet at 6 a.m. beside a small canal in Ninh Kieu District. They wear gloves and boots, and they carry large bags. Their mission is simple: to remove as much rubbish from the water as possible.

The group, called "Clean Canal Can Tho", was started in 2023 by three university friends who were tired of seeing plastic bottles and bags floating past their homes. At first, only a few neighbors joined them. Today, the group has more than 400 members on social media, and local businesses donate water and breakfast for the volunteers.

In just one morning, the volunteers can collect up to 300 kilograms of rubbish. Most of it is plastic, but they have also found old shoes, a broken chair and even a motorbike tire. The rubbish is sorted, and anything that can be recycled is sold. The money is used to buy more equipment.

"Cleaning is only half of the job," says Thao, one of the founders. "If people keep throwing rubbish into the canals, we will never finish." That is why the group also visits local schools to teach children about waste and recycling. Thao believes that if children learn good habits early, they will also change their parents' behavior.

title: Are you getting enough sleep?
text:
Most experts agree that young adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night. However, when a university in the Mekong Delta asked 300 of its students about their sleeping habits, almost half of them said they sleep fewer than six hours on weekdays. The most common reasons were studying late, using their phones in bed, and working part-time in the evening.

Lack of sleep does more than make you feel tired. It can affect your memory, so it becomes harder to remember what you learned in class. It can also make you more likely to catch colds, because your body has less time to repair itself.

So what can you do? First, try to go to bed and get up at the same time every day, even at weekends. Second, put your phone away at least 30 minutes before bed – the light from the screen tells your brain that it is still daytime. Finally, avoid drinking coffee or tea after 4 p.m.

It may seem that staying up late gives you more time to study. In fact, a good night's sleep could be the easiest way to improve your grades.
